entries.0b0b8440930cd1cb864eca7ebb21acff4b787d28: <div sID="gen1802" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Exod.19" sID="Exod.19"/> <div eID="gen1802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1803" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1804" type="x-p"/> This chapter introduces the solemnity of the giving of the law upon Mount Sinai, which was one of the most striking appearances of the divine glory that ever was in this lower world. We have here, I. The circumstances of time and place, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.1-Exod.19.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The covenant between God and Israel settled in general. The gracious proposal God made to them (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.3-Exod.19.6">ver. 3-6</reference>), and their consent to the proposal, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.7-Exod.19.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. III. Notice given three days before of God's design to give the law out of a thick cloud, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.9">ver. 9</reference>. Orders given to prepare the people to receive the law (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.10-Exod.19.13">ver. 10-13</reference>), and care taken to execute those orders, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.14-Exod.19.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. IV. A terrible appearance of God's glory upon mount Sinai, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.16-Exod.19.20">ver. 16-20</reference>. V. Silence proclaimed, and strict charges given to the people to observe decorum while God spoke to them, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.21-Exod.19.25">ver. 21</reference>, &c.
entries.f03b28770145d7044b15679a66e669f1b21d9642: <div eID="gen1804" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1803" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Covenant of Sinai. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1805" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the third month, when the children of Israel were gone forth out of the land of Egypt, the same day came they <hi type="italic">into</hi> the wilderness of Sinai. <hi type="super">2</hi> For they were departed from Rephidim, and were come <hi type="italic">to</hi> the desert of Sinai, and had pitched in the wilderness; and there Israel camped before the mount. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Moses went up unto God, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> called unto him out of the mountain, saying, Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel; <hi type="super">4</hi> Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and <hi type="italic">how</hi> I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself. <hi type="super">5</hi> Now therefore, if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me above all people: for all the earth <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine: <hi type="super">6</hi> And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation. These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the words which thou shalt speak unto the children of Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Moses came and called for the elders of the people, and laid before their faces all these words which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded him. <hi type="super">8</hi> And all the people answered together, and said, All that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken we will do. And Moses returned the words of the people unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen1805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1806" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The date of that great charter by which Israel was incorporated. 1. The time when it bears date (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.1">v. 1</reference>)—<hi type="italic">in the third month</hi> after they came out of Egypt. It is computed that the law was given just fifty days after their coming out of Egypt, in remembrance of which the feast of Pentecost was observed the fiftieth day after the passover, and in compliance with which the Spirit was poured out upon the apostles at the feast of pentecost, fifty days after the death of Christ. In Egypt they had spoken of a three days' journey into the wilderness to the place of their sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Exod.5.3">ch. v. 3</reference>), but it proved to be almost a two months' journey; so often are we out in the calculation of times, and things prove longer in the doing than we expected. 2. The place whence it bears date—from <hi type="italic">Mount Sinai,</hi> a place which nature, not art, had made eminent and conspicuous, for it was the highest in all that range of mountains. Thus God put contempt upon cities, and palaces, and magnificent structures, setting up his pavilion on the top of a high mountain, in a waste and barren desert, there to carry on this treaty. It is called <hi type="italic">Sinai,</hi> from the multitude of thorny bushes that overspread it. <div eID="gen1806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1807" type="x-p"/> II. The charter itself. Moses was called up the mountain (on the top of which God had pitched his tent, and at the foot of which Israel had pitched theirs), and was employed as the mediator, or rather no more than the messenger of the covenant: <hi type="italic">Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.3">v. 3</reference>. Here the learned bishop Patrick observes that the people are called by the names both of <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi> and <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> to remind them that those who had lately been as low as Jacob when he went to Padan-aram had now grown as great as God made him when he came thence (justly enriched with the spoils of him that had oppressed him) and was called <hi type="italic">Israel.</hi> Now observe, 1. That the maker, and first mover, of the covenant, is God himself. Nothing was said nor done by this stupid unthinking people themselves towards this settlement; no motion made, no petition put up for God's favour, but this blessed charter was granted <hi type="italic">ex mero motu—purely out of God's own good-will.</hi> Note, In all our dealings with God, free grace anticipates us with the blessings of goodness, and all our comfort is owing, not to our knowing God, but rather to our being <hi type="italic">known of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Gal. iv. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">We love him,</hi> visit him, and covenant with him, <hi type="italic">because he first loved us,</hi> visited us, and covenanted with us. God is the Alpha, and therefore must be the Omega. 2. That the matter of the covenant is not only just and unexceptionable, and such as puts no hardship upon them, but kind and gracious, and such as gives them the greatest privileges and advantages imaginable. (1.) He reminds them of what he had done for them, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.4">v. 4</reference>. He had righted them, and avenged them upon their persecutors and oppressors: "<hi type="italic">You have seen what I did unto the Egyptians,</hi> how many lives were sacrificed to Israel's honour and interests:" He had given them unparalleled instances of his favour to them, and his care of them: <hi type="italic">I bore you on eagles' wings,</hi> a high expression of the wonderful tenderness God had shown for them. It is explained, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11-Deut.32.12">Deut. xxxii. 11, 12</reference>. It denotes great speed. God not only came upon the wing for their deliverance (when the set time was come, he rode on a cherub, and did fly), but he hastened them out, as it were, upon the wing. He did it also with great ease, with the strength as well as with the swiftness of an eagle: those that faint not, nor are weary, are said to <hi type="italic">mount up with wings as eagles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa. xl. 31</reference>. Especially, it denotes God's particular care of them and affection to them. Even Egypt, that iron furnace, was the nest in which these young ones were hatched, where they were first formed as the embryo of a nation; when, by the increase of their numbers, they grew to some maturity, they were carried out of that nest. Other birds carry their young in their talons, but the eagle (they say) upon her wings, so that even those archers who shoot flying cannot hurt the young ones, unless they first shoot through the old one. Thus, in the Red Sea, the pillar of cloud and fire, the token of God's presence, interposed itself between the Israelites and their pursuers (lines of defence which could not be forced, a wall which could not be penetrated): yet this was not all; their way so paved, so guarded, was glorious, but their end much more so: <hi type="italic">I brought you unto myself.</hi> They were brought not only into a state of liberty and honour, but into covenant and communion with God. This, this was the glory of their deliverance, as it is of ours by Christ, that he died, <hi type="italic">the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.</hi> This God aims at in all the gracious methods of his providence and grace, to bring us back to himself, from whom we have revolted, and to bring us home to himself, in whom alone we can be happy. He appeals to themselves, and their own observation and experience, for the truth of what is here insisted on: <hi type="italic">You have seen what I did;</hi> so that they could not disbelieve God, unless they would first disbelieve their own eyes. They saw how all that was done was purely the Lord's doing. It was not they that reached towards God, but it was he that brought them to himself. Some have well observed that the <hi type="italic">Old-Testament church</hi> is said to be borne upon eagles' wings, denoting the power of that dispensation, which was carried on with <hi type="italic">a high hand an out-stretched arm;</hi> but the <hi type="italic">New-Testament church</hi> is said to be gathered by the Lord Jesus, <hi type="italic">as a hen gathers her chickens under her wings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>), denoting the grace and compassion of that dispensation, and the admirable condescension and humiliation of the Redeemer. (2.) He tells them plainly what he expected and required from them in one word, obedience (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">v. 5</reference>), that they should <hi type="italic">obey his voice indeed and keep his covenant.</hi> Being thus saved by him, that which he insisted upon was that they should be ruled by him. The reasonableness of this demand is, long after, pleaded with them, that <hi type="italic">in the day he brought them out of the land of Egypt</hi> this was the condition of the covenant, <hi type="italic">Obey my voice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.23">Jer. vii. 23</reference>); and this he is said to protest earnestly to them, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.4">Jer. xi. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.7">7</reference>. Only obey <hi type="italic">indeed,</hi> not in profession and promise only, not in pretence, but in sincerity. God had shown them real favours, and therefore required real obedience. (3.) He assures them of the honour he would put upon them, and the kindness he would show them, in case they did thus keep his covenant (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5-Exod.19.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then you shall be a peculiar treasure to me.</hi> He does not specify any one particular favour, as giving them the land of Canaan, or the like, but expresses it in that which was inclusive of all happiness, that he would be to them a God in covenant, and they should be to him a people. [1.] God here asserts his sovereignty over, and propriety in, the whole visible creation: <hi type="italic">All the earth is mine.</hi> Therefore he needed them not; he that had so vast a dominion was great enough, and happy enough, without concerning himself for so small a demesne as Israel was. All nations on the earth being his, he might choose which he pleased for his peculiar, and act in a way of sovereignty. [2.] He appropriates Israel to himself, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As a people dear unto him. <hi type="italic">You shall be a peculiar treasure;</hi> not that God was enriched by them, as a man is by his treasure, but he was pleased to value and esteem them as a man does his treasure; they were <hi type="italic">precious in his sight and honourable</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 4</reference>); he <hi type="italic">set his love upon them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.7">Deut. vii. 7</reference>), took them under his special care and protection, as a treasure that is kept under lock and key. He looked upon the rest of the world but as trash and lumber in comparison with them. By giving them divine revelation, instituted ordinances, and promises inclusive of eternal life, by sending his prophets among them, and pouring out his Spirit upon them, he distinguished them from, and dignified them above, all people. And this honour have all the saints; they are unto God a <hi type="italic">peculiar people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.4">Tit. ii. 14</reference>), his when he <hi type="italic">makes up his jewels. Secondly,</hi> As a people devoted to him, to his honour and service (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">v. 6</reference>), a <hi type="italic">kingdom of priests,</hi> a <hi type="italic">holy nation.</hi> All the Israelites, if compared with other people, were priests unto God, so near were they to him (<reference osisRef="Ps.148.14">Ps. cxlviii. 14</reference>), so much employed in his immediate service, and such intimate communion they had with him. When they were first made a free people it was that they might <hi type="italic">sacrifice to the Lord their God,</hi> as <hi type="italic">priests;</hi> they were under God's immediate government, and the tendency of the laws given them was to distinguish them from others, and engage them for God as a holy nation. Thus all believers are, through Christ, made to our God kings and priests (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Rev. i. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">a chosen generation, a royal priesthood,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1 Pet. ii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen1807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1808" type="x-p"/> III. Israel's acceptance of this charter, and consent to the conditions of it. 1. Moses faithfully delivered God's message to them (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.7">v. 7</reference>): He <hi type="italic">laid before their faces all those words;</hi> he not only explained to them what God had given him in charge, but he put it to their choice whether they would accept these promises upon these terms or no. His laying it to their faces denotes his laying it to their consciences. 2. They readily agreed to the covenant proposed. They would oblige themselves to obey the voice of God, and take it as a great favour to be made a kingdom of priests to him. They answered together as one man, <hi type="italic">nemine contradicente—without a dissentient voice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that the Lord hath spoken we will do.</hi> Thus they strike the bargain, accepting the Lord to be to them a God, and giving up themselves to be to him a people. O that there had been such a heart in them! 3. Moses, as a mediator, returned the words of the people to God, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.8">v. 8</reference>. Thus Christ, the Mediator between us and God, as a prophet reveals God's will to us, his precepts and promises, and then as a priest offers up to God our spiritual sacrifices, not only of prayer and praise, but of devout affections and pious resolutions, the work of his own Spirit in us. Thus he is that blessed <hi type="italic">days-man who lays his hand upon us both.</hi>
entries.dbeab06a34e165f6a95a3e073b486895b6f50d2c: <div eID="gen1808" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Approach of God Announced. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1809" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Lo, I come unto thee in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with thee, and believe thee for ever. And Moses told the words of the people unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">10</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Go unto the people, and sanctify them to day and to morrow, and let them wash their clothes, <hi type="super">11</hi> And be ready against the third day: for the third day the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will come down in the sight of all the people upon Mount Sinai. <hi type="super">12</hi> And thou shalt set bounds unto the people round about, saying, Take heed to yourselves, <hi type="italic">that ye</hi> go <hi type="italic">not</hi> up into the mount, or touch the border of it: whosoever toucheth the mount shall be surely put to death: <hi type="super">13</hi> There shall not an hand touch it, but he shall surely be stoned, or shot through; whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> beast or man, it shall not live: when the trumpet soundeth long, they shall come up to the mount. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Moses went down from the mount unto the people, and sanctified the people; and they washed their clothes. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he said unto the people, Be ready against the third day: come not at <hi type="italic">your</hi> wives. <div eID="gen1809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1810" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God intimates to Moses his purpose of coming down upon Mount Sinai, in some visible appearance of his glory, in <hi type="italic">a thick cloud</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.9">v. 9</reference>); for he said that he would <hi type="italic">dwell in the thick darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.1">2 Chron. vi. 1</reference>), and make this his pavilion (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Ps. xviii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">holding back the face of his throne</hi> when he set it upon <hi type="italic">Mount Sinai, and spreading a cloud upon it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.9">Job xxvi. 9</reference>. This thick cloud was to prohibit curious enquiries into things secret, and to command an awful adoration of that which was revealed. God would come down <hi type="italic">in the sight of all the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.11">v. 11</reference>); though they should see no manner of similitude, yet they should see so much as would convince them that God was among them of a truth. And so high was the top of Mount Sinai that it is supposed that not only the camp of Israel, but even the countries about, might discern some extraordinary appearance of glory upon it, which would strike a terror upon them. It seems also to have been particularly intended to put an honour upon Moses: <hi type="italic">That they may hear when I speak with thee, and believe thee for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.9">v. 9</reference>. Thus the correspondence was to be first settled by a sensible appearance of the divine glory, which was afterwards to be carried on more silently by the ministry of Moses. In like manner, the Holy Ghost descended visibly upon Christ at his baptism, and all that were present heard God speak to him (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>), that afterwards, without the repetition of such visible tokens, they might believe him. So likewise the Spirit descended in cloven tongues upon the apostles (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.3">Acts ii. 3</reference>), that they might be believed. Observe, When the people had declared themselves willing to obey the voice of God, then God promised they should hear his voice; for, if any man be resolved to <hi type="italic">do his will, he shall know it,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen1810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1811" type="x-p"/> II. He orders Moses to make preparation for this great solemnity, giving him two days' time for it. <div eID="gen1811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1812" type="x-p"/> 1. He must <hi type="italic">sanctify the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.10">v. 10</reference>), as Job, before this, sent and <hi type="italic">sanctified his sons,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.1.5">Job i. 5</reference>. He must raise their expectation by giving them notice what God would do, and assist their preparation by directing them what they must do. "<hi type="italic">Sanctify them,</hi>" that is, "Call them off from their worldly business, and call them to religious exercises, meditation and prayer, that they may receive the law from God's mouth with reverence and devotion. <hi type="italic">Let them be ready,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Exod.19.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, When we are to attend upon God in solemn ordinances it concerns us to sanctify ourselves, and to get ready beforehand. Wandering thoughts must be gathered in, impure affections abandoned, disquieting passions suppressed, nay, and all cares about secular business, for the present, dismissed and laid by, that our hearts may be <hi type="italic">engaged to approach unto God.</hi> Two things particularly prescribed as signs and instances of their preparation:—(1.) In token of their cleansing themselves from all sinful pollutions, that they might be holy to God, they must <hi type="italic">wash their clothes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.10">v. 10</reference>), and they did so (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.14">v. 14</reference>); not that God regards our clothes; but while they were washing their clothes he would have them think of washing their souls by repentance from the sins they had contracted in Egypt and since their deliverance. It becomes us to appear in clean clothes when we wait upon great men; so clean hearts are required in our attendance on the great God, who sees them as plainly as men see our clothes. This is absolutely necessary to our acceptably worshipping God. See <reference osisRef="Ps.26.6">Ps. xxvi. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16-Isa.1.18">Isa. i. 16-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">Heb. x. 22</reference>. (2.) In token of their devoting themselves entirely to religious exercises, upon this occasion, they must abstain even from lawful enjoyments during these three days, and not <hi type="italic">come at their wives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.15">v. 15</reference>. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.5">1 Cor. vii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen1812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1813" type="x-p"/> 2. He must <hi type="italic">set bounds about the mountain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.12-Exod.19.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. Probably he drew a line, or ditch, round at the foot of the hill, which none were to pass upon pain of death. This was to intimate, (1.) That humble awful reverence which ought to possess the minds of all those that worship God. We are mean creatures before a great Creator, vile sinners before a holy righteous Judge; and therefore a godly fear and shame well become us, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">Heb. xii. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.11">Ps. ii. 11</reference>. (2.) The distance at which worshippers were kept, under that dispensation, which we ought to take notice of, that we may the more value our privilege under the gospel, having <hi type="italic">boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.19">Heb. x. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen1813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1814" type="x-p"/> 3. He must order the people to attend upon the summons that should be given (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When the trumpet soundeth long</hi> then let them take their places at the foot of the mount, and so sit down at God's feet," as it is explained, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">Deut. xxxiii. 3</reference>. Never was so great a congregation called together, and preached to, at once, as this was here. No one man's voice could have reached so many, but the voice of God did.
entries.6b3105d531207f2650b37475a76bb3486920616e: <div eID="gen1814" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Presence on Mount Sinai. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1815" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And it came to pass on the third day in the morning, that there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud; so that all the people that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the camp trembled. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet with God; and they stood at the nether part of the mount. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> descended upon it in fire: and the smoke thereof ascended as the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mount quaked greatly. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when the voice of the trumpet sounded long, and waxed louder and louder, Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came down upon Mount Sinai, on the top of the mount: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> called Moses <hi type="italic">up</hi> to the top of the mount; and Moses went up. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Go down, charge the people, lest they break through unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to gaze, and many of them perish. <hi type="super">22</hi> And let the priests also, which come near to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , sanctify themselves, lest the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> break forth upon them. <hi type="super">23</hi> And Moses said unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai: for thou chargedst us, saying, Set bounds about the mount, and sanctify it. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto him, Away, get thee down, and thou shalt come up, thou, and Aaron with thee: but let not the priests and the people break through to come up unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , lest he break forth upon them. 25 So Moses went down unto the people, and spake unto them. <div eID="gen1815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1816" type="x-p"/> Now, at length, comes that memorable day, that terrible day of the Lord, that day of judgment, in which <hi type="italic">Israel heard the voice of the Lord God</hi> speaking to them <hi type="italic">out of the midst of the fire, and lived,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.33">Deut. iv. 33</reference>. Never was there such a sermon preached, before nor since, as this which was here preached to the church in the wilderness. For, <div eID="gen1816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1817" type="x-p"/> I. The preacher was God himself (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord descended in fire,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Lord came down upon Mount Sinai.</hi> The <hi type="italic">shechinah,</hi> or glory of the Lord, appeared in the sight of all the people; he <hi type="italic">shone forth from mount Paran with ten thousands of his saints</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deut. xxxiii. 2</reference>), that is, attended, as the divine Majesty always is, by a multitude of the holy angels, who were both to grace the solemnity and to assist at it. Hence the law is said to be given <hi type="italic">by the disposition of angels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.7.53">Acts vii. 53</reference>. <div eID="gen1817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1818" type="x-p"/> II. The pulpit (or throne rather) was mount Sinai, hung with a <hi type="italic">thick cloud</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">v. 16</reference>), covered with <hi type="italic">smoke</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.18">v. 18</reference>), and made to <hi type="italic">quake</hi> greatly. Now it was that the earth <hi type="italic">trembled at the presence of the Lord,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">mountains skipped like rams</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">Ps. cxiv. 4, 7</reference>), that Sinai itself, though rough and rocky, <hi type="italic">melted from before the Lord God of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.5.5">Judg. v. 5</reference>. Now it was that the <hi type="italic">mountains saw him, and trembled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.10">Hab. iii. 10</reference>), and were witnesses against a hard-hearted unmoved people, whom nothing would influence. <div eID="gen1818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1819" type="x-p"/> III. The congregation was called together by the <hi type="italic">sound of a trumpet, exceedingly loud</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">v. 16</reference>), and <hi type="italic">waxing louder and louder,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.19">v. 19</reference>. This was done by the ministry of the angels, and we read of trumpets sounded by angels, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.6">Rev. viii. 6</reference>. It was the <hi type="italic">sound of the trumpet that made all the people tremble,</hi> as those who knew their own guilt, and who had reason to expect that the sound of this trumpet was to them the <hi type="italic">alarm of war.</hi> <div eID="gen1819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1820" type="x-p"/> IV. Moses brought the hearers to the place of meeting, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.17">v. 17</reference>. He that had led them out of the bondage of Egypt now led them to receive the law from God's mouth. Public persons are indeed public blessings when they lay out themselves in their places to promote the public worship of God. Moses, at the head of an assembly worshipping God, was as truly great as Moses at the head of an army in the field. <div eID="gen1820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1821" type="x-p"/> V. The introductions to the service were <hi type="italic">thunders and lightnings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">v. 16</reference>. These were designed to strike an awe upon the people, and to raise and engage their attention. Were they asleep? The thunders would awaken them. Were they looking another way? The lightnings would engage them to turn their faces towards him that spoke to them. Thunder and lightning have natural causes, but the scripture directs us in a particular manner to take notice of the power of God, and his terror, in them. Thunder is the voice of God, and lightning the fire of God, proper to engage the senses of sight and hearing, those senses by which we receive so much of our information. <div eID="gen1821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1822" type="x-p"/> VI. Moses is God's minister, who is spoken to, to command silence, and keep the congregation in order: <hi type="italic">Moses spoke,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.19">v. 19</reference>. Some think it was now that he said, <hi type="italic">I exceedingly fear and quake</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.21">Heb. xii. 21</reference>); but God stilled his fear by his distinguishing favour to him, in calling him up to the top of the mount (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.20">v. 20</reference>), by which also he tried his faith and courage. No sooner had Moses got up a little way towards the top of the mount than he was sent down again to keep the people from <hi type="italic">breaking through to gaze,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.21">v. 21</reference>. Even the priests or princes, the heads of the houses of their fathers, who officiated for their respective families, and therefore are said to <hi type="italic">come near to the Lord</hi> at other times, must now keep their distance, and conduct themselves with a great deal of caution. Moses pleads that they needed not to have any further orders given them, effectual care being taken already to prevent any intrusions, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.23">v. 23</reference>. But God, who knew their wilfulness and presumption, and what was now in the hearts of some of them, hastens him down with this in charge, that neither the priests nor the people should offer to force the lines that were set, to <hi type="italic">come up unto the Lord,</hi> but Moses and Aaron on, the men whom God delighted to honour. Observe, 1. What it was that God forbade them—breaking through to gaze; enough was provided to awaken their consciences, but they were not allowed to gratify their vain curiosity. They might see, but not gaze. Some of them, probably, were desirous to see some similitude, that they might know how to make an image of God, which he took care to prevent, for they <hi type="italic">saw no manner of similitude,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.5">Deut. iv. 5</reference>. Note, In divine things we must not covet to know more than God would have us know; and he has allowed us as much as is good for us. A desire of forbidden knowledge was the ruin of our first parents. Those that would be wise above what is written, and intrude into those things which they have not seen, need this admonition, that they <hi type="italic">break not through to gaze.</hi> 2. Under what penalty it was forbidden: <hi type="italic">Lest the Lord break forth upon them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.22-Exod.19.24">v. 22-24</reference>), and <hi type="italic">many of them perish.</hi> Note, (1.) The restraints and warnings of the divine law are all intended for our good, and to keep us out of that danger into which we should otherwise, by our own folly, run ourselves. (2.) It is at our peril if we break the bounds that God has set us, and intrude upon that which he has not allowed us; the Bethshemites and Uzzah paid dearly for their presumption. And, even when we are called to approach God, we must remember that he is in heaven and we upon earth, and therefore it behoves us to exercise reverence and godly fear.  <chapter eID="Exod.19"/> <div eID="gen1822" type="x-p"/>

entries.adfa1095536b7c06075f14de31692d6258e2ac4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv777"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.19.1-Exod.19.25">Ex 19:1-25</reference>. Arrival at Sinai.</title> <div sID="gen1094" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv777"/><hi type="bold">1. In the third month--</hi>according to Jewish usage, the first day of that month--"same day."--It is added, to mark the time more explicitly, that is, forty-five days after Egypt--one day spent on the mount (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.3">Ex 19:3</reference>), one returning the people's answer (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.7">Ex 19:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.8">8</reference>), three days of preparation, making the whole time fifty days from the first passover to the promulgation of the law. Hence the feast of pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day, was the inauguration of the Old Testament church, and the divine wisdom is apparent in the selection of the same reason for the institution of the New Testament church (<reference osisRef="John.1.17">Joh 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.1">Ac 2:1</reference>). <div eID="gen1094" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ac8f5f6e3f954d4eb246534e281ea48a6beabc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv778"/><div sID="gen1095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv778"/><hi type="bold">2. were come to the desert of Sinai--</hi>The desert has its provinces, or divisions, distinguished by a variety of names; and the "desert of Sinai" is that wild and desolate region which occupies the very center of the peninsula, comprising the lofty range to which the mount of God belongs. It is a wilderness of shaggy rocks of porphyry and red granite, and of valleys for the most part bare of verdure.<div eID="gen1095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and there Israel camped before the mount--</hi>Sinai, so called from Seneh, or acacia bush. It is now called Jebel Musa. Their way into the interior of the gigantic cluster was by Wady Feiran, which would lead the bulk of the hosts with their flocks and herds into the high valleys of Jebel Musa, with their abundant springs, especially into the great thoroughfare of the desert--the longest, widest, and most continuous of all the valleys, the Wady-es-Sheikh, while many would be scattered among the adjacent valleys; so that thus secluded from the world in a wild and sublime amphitheatre of rocks, they "camped before the mount." "In this valley--a long flat valley--about a quarter of a mile in breadth, winding northwards, Israel would find ample room for their encampment. Of all the wadys in that region, it seems the most suitable for a prolonged sojourn. The 'goodly tents' of Israel could spread themselves without limit" [Bonar]. <div eID="gen1096" type="x-p"/>
entries.6183bdfea2a801cbce9aafa6aca5b4d76de59827: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv779"/><div sID="gen1097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv779"/><hi type="bold">3-6. Moses went up unto God--</hi>the Shekinah--within the cloud (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.20">Ex 33:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>).<div eID="gen1097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, &c.--</hi>The object for which Moses went up was to receive and convey to the people the message contained in these verses, and the purport of which was a general announcement of the terms on which God was to take the Israelites into a close and peculiar relation to Himself. In thus negotiating between God and His people, the highest post of duty which any mortal man was ever called to occupy, Moses was still but a servant. The only Mediator is Jesus Christ [1Ti 2:5; He 12:24]. <div eID="gen1098" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3ebac3737e6c1b4a21bfa1b23b35366bd33bdbb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv781"/><div sID="gen1101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv781"/><hi type="bold">7-8. Moses came and called for the elders of the people--</hi>The message was conveyed to the mighty multitude through their elders, who, doubtless, instructed them in the conditions required. Their unanimous acceptance was conveyed through the same channel to Moses, and by him reported to the Lord. Ah! how much self-confidence did their language betray! How little did they know what spirit they were of! <div eID="gen1101" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a01a89a9c874217870dda69eeb3674c7b2cf018: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv782"/><div sID="gen1102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv782"/><hi type="bold">9-15. The Lord said unto Moses, Lo, I come ... in a thick cloud, &c.--</hi>The deepest impressions are made on the mind through the medium of the senses; and so He who knew what was in man signalized His descent at the inauguration of the ancient church, by all the sensible tokens of august majesty that were fitted to produce the conviction that He is the great and terrible God. The whole multitude must have anticipated the event with feelings of intense solemnity and awe. The extraordinary preparations enjoined, the ablutions and rigid abstinence they were required to observe, the barriers erected all round the base of the mount, and the stern penalties annexed to the breach of any of the conditions, all tended to create an earnest and solemn expectation which increased as the appointed day drew near. <div eID="gen1102" type="x-p"/>
entries.89b7b64cdebe243374f78980613912c013ff982a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv783"/><div sID="gen1103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv783"/><hi type="bold">16. on the third day in the morning, that there were thunders and lightnings, &c.--</hi>The descent of God was signalized by every object imagination can conceive connected with the ideas of grandeur and of awe. But all was in keeping with the character of the law about to be proclaimed. As the mountain burned with fire, God was exhibited as a consuming fire to the transgressors of His law. The thunder and lightning, more awful amid the deep stillness of the region and reverberating with terrific peals among the mountains, would rouse the universal attention; a thick cloud was an apt emblem of the dark and shadowy dispensation (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">Mt 17:5</reference>).<div eID="gen1103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the voice of a trumpet--</hi>This gave the scene the character of a miraculous transaction, in which other elements than those of nature were at work, and some other than material trumpet was blown by other means than human breath. <div eID="gen1104" type="x-p"/>
entries.64e46b8aa8ac8742f3071d9006658d54e90d5e5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv784"/><div sID="gen1105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv784"/><hi type="bold">17. Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet with God--</hi>Wady-er-Raheh, where they stood, has a spacious sandy plain; immediately in front of Es Suksafeh, considered by Robinson to be the mount from which the law was given. "We measured it, and estimate the whole plain at two geographical miles long, and ranging in breadth from one-third to two-thirds of a mile, or as equivalent to a surface of one square mile. This space is nearly doubled by the recess on the west, and by the broad and level area of Wady-es-Sheikh on the east, which issues at right angles to the plain, and is equally in view of the front and summit of the mount. The examination convinced us that here was space enough to satisfy all the requisitions of the Scripture narrative, so far as it relates to the assembling of the congregation to receive the law. Here, too, one can see the fitness of the injunction to set bounds around the mount, that neither man nor beast might approach too near, for it rises like a perpendicular wall." But Jebel Musa, the old traditional Sinai, and the highest peak, has also a spacious valley, Wady Sebaiyeh, capable of holding the people. It is not certain on which of these two they stood. <div eID="gen1105" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f9b47492e9b40219c0fa653167cbdf70b503752: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv785"/><div sID="gen1106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv785"/><hi type="bold">21. the Lord said unto Moses, Go down, charge the people--</hi>No sooner had Moses proceeded a little up the mount, than he was suddenly ordered to return, in order to keep the people from breaking through to gaze--a course adopted to heighten the impressive solemnity of the scene. The strict injunctions renewed to all, whatever their condition, at a time and in circumstances when the whole multitude of Israel were standing at the base of the mount, was calculated in the highest degree to solemnize and awe every heart. <chapter eID="Exod.19"/>

entries.332e315d9f2d81227079e0b1217ef098a20d938f: <div eID="gen3227" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen3228" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3229" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3229" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3228" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3230" type="x-p"/> The children of Israel, having departed from Rephidim, come to the wilderness of Sinai in the third month, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.1">Exo 19:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.2">Exo 19:2</reference>. Moses goes up into the mount to God, and receives a message which he is to deliver to the people, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.3-Exo.19.6">Exo 19:3-6</reference>. He returns and delivers it to the people before the elders, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.7">Exo 19:7</reference>. The people promise obedience, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.8">Exo 19:8</reference>. The Lord proposes to meet Moses in the cloud, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.9">Exo 19:9</reference>. He commands him to sanctify the people, and promises to come down visibly on Mount Sinai on the third day, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.10">Exo 19:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.11">Exo 19:11</reference>. He commands him also to set bounds, to prevent the people or any of the cattle from touching the mount, on pain of being stoned or shot through with a dart, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.12">Exo 19:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.13">Exo 19:13</reference>. Moses goes down and delivers this message, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.14">Exo 19:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.15">Exo 19:15</reference>. The third day is ushered in with the appearance of the thick cloud upon the mount, and with thunders, lightning, and the sound of a trumpet! at which the people are greatly terrified, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.16">Exo 19:16</reference> <div eID="gen3230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3231" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen3231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3232" type="x-p"/> In the third month - This was called Sivan, and answers to our May. For the Jewish months, years, etc. <div eID="gen3232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3233" type="x-p"/> The same day - There are three opinions concerning the meaning of this place, which are supported by respectable arguments. <div eID="gen3233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3234" type="x-p"/> 1. The same day means the same day of the third month with that, viz., the 15th, on which the Israelites had left Egypt. <div eID="gen3234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3235" type="x-p"/> 2. The same day signifies here a day of the same number with the month to which it is applied, viz., the third day of the third month. <div eID="gen3235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3236" type="x-p"/> 3. By the same day, the first day of the month is intended. The Jews celebrate the feast of pentecost fifty days after the passover: from the departure out of Egypt to the coming to Sinai were forty-five days; for they came out the fifteenth day of the first month, from which day to the first of the third month forty-five days are numbered. On the 2d day of this third month Moses went up into the mountain, when three days were given to the people to purify themselves; this gives the fourth day of the third month, or the forty-ninth from the departure out of Egypt. On the next day, which was the fiftieth from the celebration of the passover, the glory of God appeared on the mount; in commemoration of which the Jews celebrate the feast of pentecost. This is the opinion of St. Augustine and of several moderns, and is defended at large by Houbigant. As the word חדש chodesh, month, is put for new moon, which is with the Jews the first day of the month, this may be considered an additional confirmation of the above opinion. <div eID="gen3236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3237" type="x-p"/> The wilderness of Sinai - Mount Sinai is called by the Arabs Jibel Mousa or the Mount of Moses, or, by way of eminence, El Tor, The Mount. It is one hill, with two peaks or summits; one is called Horeb, the other Sinai. Horeb was probably its most ancient name, and might designate the whole mountain; but as the Lord had appeared to Moses on this mountain in a bush סנה seneh, <reference osisRef="Exo.3.2">Exo 3:2</reference>, from this circumstance it might have received the name of Sinai or הר סיני har Sinai, the mount of the bush or the mount of bushes; for it is possible that it was not in a single bush, but in a thicket of bushes, that the Angel of God made his appearance. The word bush is often used for woods or forests.
entries.1481db6468d7d05487276a95a197cb359b9cc9c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen3237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3238" type="x-p"/> Moses went up unto God - It is likely that the cloud which had conducted the Israelitish camp had now removed to the top of Sinai; and as this was the symbol of the Divine presence, Moses went up to the place, there to meet the Lord. <div eID="gen3238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3239" type="x-p"/> The Lord called unto him - This, according to St. Stephen, was the Angel of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Act.7.38">Act 7:38</reference>. And from several scriptures we have seen that the Lord Jesus was the person intended; see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.16.7">Gen 16:7</reference>; see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.18.13">Gen 18:13</reference>; see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.3.2">Exo 3:2</reference>.
entries.a1bbe08a24fb3fd47af48952e79992bf191c1891: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen3239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3240" type="x-p"/> How I bare you on eagles' wings - Mr. Bruce contends that the word נשר nesher does not mean the bird we term eagle; but a bird which the Arabs, from its kind and merciful disposition, call rachama, which is noted for its care of its young, and its carrying them upon its back. See his Travels, vol. vii., pl. 33. It is not unlikely that from this part of the sacred history the heathens borrowed their fable of the eagle being a bird sacred to Jupiter, and which was employed to carry the souls of departed heroes, kings, etc., into the celestial regions. The Romans have struck several medals with this device, which may be seen in different cabinets, among which are the following: one of Faustina, daughter of Antoninus Pius, on the reverse of which she is represented ascending to heaven on the back of an eagle; and another of Salonia, daughter of the Emperor Galienus, on the reverse of which she is represented on the back of an eagle, with a scepter in her hand, ascending to heaven. Jupiter himself is sometimes represented on the back of an eagle also, with his thunder in his hand, as on a medal of Licinus. This brings us nearer to the letter of the text, where it appears that the heathens confounded the figure made use of by the sacred penman, I bare you on eagles' wings, with the manifestation of God in thunder and lightning on Mount Sinai. And it might be in reference to all this that the Romans took the eagle for their ensign. See Scheuchzer, Fusellius, etc. <div eID="gen3240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3241" type="x-p"/> Brought you unto myself - In this and the two following verses, we see the design of God in selecting a people for himself. <div eID="gen3241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3242" type="x-p"/> 1. They were to obey his voice, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.5">Exo 19:5</reference>, to receive a revelation from him, and to act according to that revelation, and not according to their reason or fancy, in opposition to his declarations. <div eID="gen3242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3243" type="x-p"/> 2. They were to obey his voice indeed, שמוע תשמעו shamoa tishmeu, in hearing they should hear; they should consult his testimonies, hear them whenever read or proclaimed, and obey them as soon as heard, affectionately and steadily. <div eID="gen3243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3244" type="x-p"/> 3. They must keep his covenant - not only copy in their lives the ten commandments, but they must receive and preserve the grand agreement made between God and man by sacrifice, in reference to the incarnation and death of Christ; for from the foundation of the world the covenant of God ratified by sacrifices referred to this, and now the sacrificial system was to be more fully opened by the giving of the law. <div eID="gen3244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3245" type="x-p"/> 4. They should then be God's peculiar treasure, סגלה segullah, his own patrimony, a people in whom he should have all right, and over whom he should have exclusive authority above all the people of the earth; for though all the inhabitants of the world were his by his right of creation and providence, yet these should be peculiarly his, as receiving his revelation and entering into his covenant. <div eID="gen3245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3246" type="x-p"/> 5. They should be a kingdom of priests, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.6">Exo 19:6</reference>. Their state should be a theocracy; and as God should be the sole governor, being king in Jeshurun, so all his subjects should be priests, all worshippers, all sacrificers, every individual offering up the victim for himself. A beautiful representation of the Gospel dispensation, to which the Apostles Peter and John apply it, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pet 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pet 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Rev 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.10">Rev 5:10</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Rev.20.6">Rev 20:6</reference>; under which dispensation every believing soul offers up for himself that Lamb of God which was slain for and which takes away the sin of the world, and through which alone a man can have access to God.
entries.3dff7692478cb8415368a6524af4951b9614d8c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen3246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3247" type="x-p"/> And a holy nation - They should be a nation, one people; firmly united among themselves, living under their own laws; and powerful, because united, and acting under the direction and blessing of God. They should be a holy nation, saved from their sins, righteous in their conduct, holy in their hearts; every external rite being not only a significant ceremony, but also a means of conveying light and life, grace and peace, to every person who conscientiously used it. Thus they should be both a kingdom, having God for their governor; and a nation, a multitude of peoples connected together; not a scattered, disordered, and disorganized people, but a royal nation, using their own rites, living under their own laws, subject in religious matters only to God, and in things civil, to every ordinance of man for God's sake. <div eID="gen3247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3248" type="x-p"/> This was the spirit and design of this wonderful institution, which could not receive its perfection but under the Gospel, and has its full accomplishment in every member of the mystical body of Christ.
entries.8a15663c2cacc8a5096e69cae526602c97fdbd0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen3248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3249" type="x-p"/> The elders of the people - The head of each tribe, and the chief of each family, by whose ministry this gracious purpose of God was speedily communicated to the whole camp.
entries.c3ff4f3415bea8ac8fa51b8ef308348226780c43: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen3249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3250" type="x-p"/> And all the people answered, etc. - The people, having such gracious advantages laid before them, most cheerfully consented to take God for their portion; as he had graciously promised to take them for his people. Thus a covenant was made, the parties being mutually bound to each other. <div eID="gen3250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3251" type="x-p"/> Moses returned the words - When the people had on their part consented to the covenant, Moses appears to have gone immediately up to the mountain and related to God the success of his mission; for he was now on the mount, as appears from <reference osisRef="Exo.19.14">Exo 19:14</reference>.
entries.7f645efee9f51a20c5382b5b71d94c33a147fba3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen3251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3252" type="x-p"/> A thick cloud - This is interpreted by <reference osisRef="Exo.19.18">Exo 19:18</reference> : And Mount Sinai was altogether on a Smoke - and the Smoke thereof ascended as the Smoke of a furnace; his usual appearance was in the cloudy pillar, which we may suppose was generally clear and luminous. That the people may hear - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.15.9">Exo 15:9</reference>. The Jews consider this as the fullest evidence their fathers had of the Divine mission of Moses; themselves were permitted to see this awfully glorious sight, and to hear God himself speak out of the thick darkness: for before this, as Rabbi Maymon remarks, they might have thought that Moses wrought his miracles by sorcery or enchantment; but now, hearing the voice of God himself, they could no longer disbelieve nor even doubt.
entries.1eec99db6b770bec0465968b04c3bebbefd12eb5: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen3252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3253" type="x-p"/> Sanctify them - See the meaning of this term, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.2">Exo 13:2</reference>. <div eID="gen3253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3254" type="x-p"/> Let them wash their clothes - And consequently bathe their bodies; for, according to the testimony of the Jews, these always went together. <div eID="gen3254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3255" type="x-p"/> It was necessary that, as they were about to appear in the presence of God, every thing should be clean and pure about them; that they might be admonished by this of the necessity of inward purity, of which the outward washing was the emblem. <div eID="gen3255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3256" type="x-p"/> From these institutions the heathens appear to have borrowed their precepts relative to washings and purifications previously to their offering sacrifice to their gods, examples of which abound in the Greek and Latin writers. They washed their hands and clothes, and bathed their bodies in pure water, before they performed any act of religious worship; and in a variety of cases, abstinence from all matrimonial connections was positively required, before a person was permitted to perform any religious rite, or assist at the performance.
entries.ae534f217b1fe95e81f623a58e088fe2663e8c35: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen3256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3257" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt set bounds - Whether this was a line marked out on the ground, beyond which they were not to go, or whether a fence was actually made to keep them off, we cannot tell; or whether this fence was made all round the mountain, or only at that part to which one wing of the camp extended, is not evident. <div eID="gen3257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3258" type="x-p"/> This verse strictly forbids the people from coming near and touching Mount Sinai, which was burning with Fire. The words therefore in <reference osisRef="Exo.19.15">Exo 19:15</reference>, אל תגשו אל אשה al tiggeshu el ishshah, come not at your wives, seem rather to mean, come not near unto the Fire; especially as the other phrase is not at all probable: but the fire is, on this occasion, spoken of so emphatically (see <reference osisRef="Deu.5.4">Deu 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.5.5">Deu 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.5.22-Deu.5.25">Deu 5:22-25</reference>) that we are naturally led to consider אשה ishshah here as האש ha-esh transposed, or to say, with Simon in his Lexicon, אשה faem, idem quod masc. אש ignis. So among other instances, we have אבר and אברה a wing; אור and אורה light; אמץ and אמצה strength; and אמר and אמרה a speech - Burt. See Kennicott's Remarks. <div eID="gen3258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3259" type="x-p"/> Whosoever toucheth the mount shall be surely put to death - The place was awfully sacred, because the dreadful majesty of God was displayed on it. And this taught them that God is a consuming fire, and that it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
entries.c352b4a15b3988f7c2de5ff248dd93169bc21528: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen3259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3260" type="x-p"/> There shall not a hand touch it - בו bo, Him, not the mountain, but the man who had presumed to touch the mountain. He should be considered altogether as an unclean and accursed thing, not to be touched for fear of conveying defilement; but should be immediately stoned or pierced through with a dart, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.20">Heb 12:20</reference>.
entries.04c87ee7f08a9dc3b9c92718e69249b817df3bb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen3260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3261" type="x-p"/> Thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud - and the voice of the trumpet - The thunders, lightnings, etc., announced the coming, as they proclaimed the majesty, of God. Of the thunders and lightnings, and the deep, dark, dismal, electric cloud, from which the thunders and lightnings proceeded, we can form a tolerable apprehension; but of the loud, long-sounding trumpet, we can scarcely form a conjecture. Such were the appearances and the noise that all the people in the camp trembled, and Moses himself was constrained to say, "I exceedingly fear and quake," <reference osisRef="Heb.12.21">Heb 12:21</reference>. Probably the sound of the trumpet was something similar to that which shall be blown by the angel when he sweareth, by Him that liveth for ever, There shall be time no longer!
entries.3a6a051cb458e53500264c2dc2275a4b4d443d50: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen3261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3262" type="x-p"/> And Moses brought forth the people - to meet with God - For though they might not touch the mount till they had permission, yet when the trumpet sounded long, it appears they might come up to the nether part of the mount, (see <reference osisRef="Exo.19.13">Exo 19:13</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deu.4.11">Deu 4:11</reference>); and when the trumpet had ceased to sound, they might then go up unto the mountain, as to any other place. <div eID="gen3262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3263" type="x-p"/> It was absolutely necessary that God should give the people at large some particular evidence of his being and power, that they might be saved from idolatry, to which they were most deplorably prone; and that they might the more readily credit Moses, who was to be the constant mediator between God and them. God, therefore, in his indescribable majesty, descended on the mount; and, by the thick dark cloud, the violent thunders, the vivid lightnings, the long and loud blasts of the trumpet, the smoke encompassing the whole mountain, and the excessive earthquake, proclaimed his power, his glory, and his holiness; so that the people, however unfaithful and disobedient afterwards, never once doubted the Divine interference, or suspected Moses of any cheat or imposture. Indeed, so absolute and unequivocal were the proofs of supernatural agency, that it was impossible these appearances could be attributed to any cause but the unlimited power of the author of Nature. <div eID="gen3263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3264" type="x-p"/> It is worthy of remark that the people were informed three days before, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.9-Exo.19.11">Exo 19:9-11</reference>, that such an appearance was to take place; and this answered two excellent purposes: <div eID="gen3264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3265" type="x-p"/> 1. They had time to sanctify and prepare themselves for this solemn transaction; and, <div eID="gen3265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3266" type="x-p"/> 2. Those who might be skeptical had sufficient opportunity to make use of every precaution to prevent and detect an imposture; so this previous warning strongly serves the cause of Divine revelation. <div eID="gen3266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3267" type="x-p"/> Their being at first prohibited from touching the mount on the most awful penalties, and secondly, being permitted to see manifestations of the Divine majesty, and hear the words of God, subserved the same great purposes. Their being prohibited in the first instance would naturally whet their curiosity, make them cautious of being deceived, and ultimately impress them with a due sense of God's justice and their own sinfulness; and their being permitted afterwards to go up to the mount, must have deepened the conviction that all was fair and real, that there could be no imposture in the case, and that though the justice and purity of God forbade them to draw nigh for a time, yet his mercy, which had prescribed the means of purification, had permitted an access to his presence. The directions given from <reference osisRef="Exo.19.10-Exo.19.15">Exo 19:10-15</reference> inclusive show, not only the holiness of God, but the purity he requires in his worshippers. <div eID="gen3267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3268" type="x-p"/> Besides, the whole scope and design of the chapter prove that no soul can possibly approach this holy and terrible Being but through a mediator; and this is the use made of this whole transaction by the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18-Heb.12.24">Heb 12:18-24</reference>.
entries.fc9d0dc13fd924422a06a8dde45d6299dda3217b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen3268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3269" type="x-p"/> The Lord came down - This was undoubtedly done in a visible manner, that the people might witness the awful appearance. We may suppose that every thing was arranged thus: the glory of the Lord occupied the top of the mountain, and near to this Moses was permitted to approach. Aaron and the seventy elders were permitted to advance some way up the mountain, while the people were only permitted to come up to its base. Moses, as the lawgiver, was to receive the statutes and judgments from God's mouth; Aaron and the elders were to receive them from Moses, and deliver them to the people; and the people were to act according to the direction received. Nothing can be imagined more glorious, terrible, majestic, and impressive, than the whole of this transaction; but it was chiefly calculated to impress deep reverence, religious fear, and sacred awe; and he who attempts to worship God uninfluenced by these, has neither a proper sense of the Divine majesty, nor of the sinfulness of sin. It seems in reference to this that the apostle says, Let us have grace whereby we may serve God acceptably with Reverence and Godly Fear: for our God is a Consuming Fire; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">Heb 12:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.29">Heb 12:29</reference>. Who then shall dare to approach him in his own name and without a mediator?
entries.c142b744589f1f39432ab28383fa990b4690c291: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen3269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3270" type="x-p"/> Let the priests also - sanctify themselves - That there were priests among the Hebrews before the consecration of Aaron and his sons, cannot be doubted; though their functions might be in a considerable measure suspended while under persecution in Egypt, yet the persons existed whose right and duty it was to offer sacrifices to God. Moses requested liberty from Pharaoh to go into the wilderness to sacrifice; and had there not been among the people both sacrifices and priests, the request itself must have appeared nugatory and absurd. Sacrifices from the beginning had constituted an essential part of the worship of God, and there certainly were priests whose business it was to offer them to God before the giving of the law; though this, for especial reasons, was restricted to Aaron and his sons after the law had been given. As sacrifices had not been offered for a considerable time, the priests themselves were considered in a state of impurity; and therefore God requires that they also should be purified for the purpose of approaching the mountain, and hearing their Maker promulgate his laws. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.28.1">Exo 28:1</reference>.
entries.526f540ad5678f44054cf275d082c31acb5f1853: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen3270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3271" type="x-p"/> The people cannot come up - Either because they had been so solemnly forbidden that they would not dare, with the penalty of instant death before their eyes, to transgress the Divine command; or the bounds which were set about the mount were such as rendered their passing them physically impossible. <div eID="gen3271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3272" type="x-p"/> And sanctify it - וקדשהי vekiddashio. Here the word קדש kadash is taken in its proper literal sense, signifying the separating of a thing, person or place, from all profane or common uses, and devoting it to sacred purposes.
entries.bd4bc07fe0e459e2852fb22d72b1c823e2c58f61: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen3272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3273" type="x-p"/> Let not the priests and the people break through - God knew that they were heedless, criminally curious, and stupidly obstinate; and therefore his mercy saw it right to give them line upon line, that they might not transgress to their own destruction. <div eID="gen3273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3274" type="x-p"/> From the very solemn and awful manner in which the Law was introduced, we may behold it as the ministration of terror and death, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7">2Cor 3:7</reference>, appearing rather to exclude men from God than to bring them nigh; and from this we may learn that an approach to God would have been for ever impossible, had not infinite mercy found out the Gospel scheme of salvation. By this, and this alone, we draw nigh to God; for we have an entrance into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.19">Heb 10:19</reference>. "For," says the apostle, "ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire; nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest, and to the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which voice they that heard entreated that the word should not be spoken to them any more, (for they could not endure that which was commanded, And if so much as a beast touch the mountain it shall be stoned, or thrust through with a dart: and so terrible was the sight that Moses said, I exceedingly fear and quake): but ye are come unto Mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and Church of the first-born, which are written in heaven; and to God, the Judge of all; and to the spirits of just men made perfect; and to Jesus the Mediator of the New Covenant; and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel;" <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18-Heb.12.24">Heb 12:18-24</reference>. Reader, art thou still under the influence and condemning power of that fiery law which proceeded from his right hand? Art thou yet afar off? Remember, thou canst only come nigh by the blood of sprinkling; and till justified by his blood, thou art under the curse. Consider the terrible majesty of God. If thou have his favor thou hast life; if his frown, death. Be instantly reconciled to God, for though thou hast deeply sinned, and he is just, yet he is the justifier of him that believeth in Christ Jesus. Believe on him, receive his salvation, Obey his voice indeed, and Keep his covenant, and Then shalt thou be a king and a priest unto God and the Lamb, and be finally saved with all the power of an endless life. Amen.  <chapter eID="Exod.19"/> <div eID="gen3274" type="x-p"/>

entries.c3072530dcbf3bbaadc2da679f08cf51e96b1e92: <reference osisRef="Exod.19.1-Exod.19.2">Exo 19:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen867" type="x-p"/> In the third month after their departure from Egypt, the Israelites arrived at Sinai, proceeding from Rephidim into the desert of Sinai, and encamping there before the mountain. On what day of the month, the received text does not state. The striking expression הזּה בּיּום (“the same day”), without any previous notice of the day, cannot signify the first day of the month; nor can השּׁלישׁי החדשׁ signify the third new moon in the year, and be understood as referring to the first day of the third month. For although, according to the etymology of חדשׁ (from חדשׁ to be new), it might denote the new moon, yet in chronological data it is never used in this sense; but the day of the month is invariably appended after the month itself has been given (e.g., לחדשׁ אחד <reference osisRef="Exod.40.2">Exo 40:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.40.17">Exo 40:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.8.5">Gen 8:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.13">Gen 8:13</reference>; Num 1:1; Num 29:1; Num 33:38, etc.). Moreover, in the Pentateuch the word חדשׁ never signifies new moon; but the new moons are called חדשׁים ראשׁי (Num 10:10; Num 28:11, cf. Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Dissertations</hi>, vol. ii. 297). And even in such passages as <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.5">1Sa 20:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.24">1Sa 18:24</reference>; 2Ki 4:23; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Amo 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa 1:13</reference>, etc., where חדשׁ is mentioned as a feast along with the Sabbaths and other feasts, the meaning new moon appears neither demonstrable nor necessary, as חדשׁ in this case denotes the feast of the month, the celebration of the beginning of the month. If, therefore, the text is genuine, and the date of the month has not dropt out (and the agreement of the ancient versions with the Masoretic text favours this conclusion), there is no other course open, than to understand יום, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Gen 2:4</reference> and Num 3:1, and probably also in the unusual expression החדשׁ יום, <reference osisRef="Exod.40.2">Exo 40:2</reference>, in the general sense of time; so that here, and also in Num 9:1; Num 20:1, the month only is given, and not the day of the month, and it is altogether uncertain whether the arrival in the desert of Sinai took place on one of the first, one of the middle, or one of the last days of the month. The Jewish tradition, which assigns the giving of the law to the fiftieth day after the Passover, is of far too recent a date to pass for historical (see my <hi type="italic">Archäologie</hi>, §83, 6). <div eID="gen867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen868" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">desert of Sinai</hi> is not the plain of er Rahah to the north of Horeb, but the desert in front (נגד) of the mountain, upon the summit of which Jehovah came down, whilst Moses ascended it to receive the law (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.20">Exo 19:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.34.2">Exo 34:2</reference>). This mountain is constantly called Sinai so long as Israel stayed there (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.18">Exo 19:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.20">Exo 19:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.23">Exo 19:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.24.16">Exo 24:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.2">Exo 34:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.4">Exo 34:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.29">Exo 34:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.32">Exo 34:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.7.38">Lev 7:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.1">Lev 25:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.46">Lev 26:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.27.34">Lev 27:34</reference>; Num 3:1; see also Num 28:6 and <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deu 33:2</reference>); and the place of their encampment by the mountain is also called the “<hi type="italic">desert of Sinai,</hi>” never the desert of Horeb (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.38">Lev 7:38</reference>; Num 1:1, Num 1:19; Num 3:14; Num 9:1; Num 10:12; Num 26:64; Num 33:15). But in <reference osisRef="Exod.33.6">Exo 33:6</reference> this spot is designated as “Mount Horeb,” and in Deuteronomy, as a rule, it is spoken of briefly as “Horeb” (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.2">Deu 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.6">Deu 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.19">Deu 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.10">Deu 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.15">Deu 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.2">Deu 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.8">Deu 9:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.16">Deu 18:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.1">Deu 29:1</reference>). And whilst the general identity of Sinai and Horeb may be inferred from this; the fact, that wherever the intention of the writer is to give a precise and geographical description of the place where the law was given, the name Sinai is employed, leads to the conclusion that the term Horeb was more general and comprehensive than that of Sinai; in other words, that Horeb was the range of which Sinai was one particular mountain, which only came prominently out to view when Israel had arrived at the mount of legislation. This distinction between the two names, which Hengstenberg was the first to point out and establish (in his <hi type="italic">Dissertations</hi>, vol. ii. p. 325), is now generally admitted; so that the only room that is left for any difference of opinion is with reference to the extent of the <hi type="italic">Horeb</hi> range. There is no ground for supposing that the name Horeb includes the whole of the mountains in the Arabian peninsula. Sufficient justice is done to all the statements in the Bible, if we restrict this name to the southern and highest range of the central mountains-to the exclusion, therefore, of the Serbal group.<note placement="foot">This hypothesis advocated by <hi type="italic">Lepsius</hi>, that Sinai or Horeb is to be sought for in Serbal, has very properly met with no favour. For the objections to this, see <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdkunde 14, pp. 738ff.; and <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi>, History of O.C., vol. iii. p. 94ff.</note> <div eID="gen868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen869" type="x-p"/> This southern range, which Arabian geographers and the Bedouins call <hi type="italic">Jebel Tur</hi> or <hi type="italic">Jebel</hi> <hi type="italic">Tur Sina</hi>, consists of three summits: (1) a central one, called by the Arabs <hi type="italic">Jebel Musa</hi> (Moses’ Mountain), and by Christians either <hi type="italic">Horeb</hi> or else <hi type="italic">Horeb-Sinai</hi>, in which case the northern and lower peak, or <hi type="italic">Ras es Sufsafeh</hi>, is called Horeb, and the southern and loftier one Sinai; (2) a western one, called <hi type="italic">Jebel Humr</hi>, with <hi type="italic">Mount Catherine</hi> on the south, the loftiest point in the whole range; and (3) an eastern one, called <hi type="italic">Jebel el Deir</hi> (Convent Mountain) or <hi type="italic">Episteme</hi> (<hi type="italic">vide Ritter</hi>, 14, pp. 527ff.). - Near this range there are two plains, which furnish space enough for a large encampment. One of these is the plain of <hi type="italic">er Rahah</hi>, on the north and north-west of Horeb-Sinai, with a level space of an English square mile, which is considerably enlarged by the Sheikh valley that opens into it from the east. At its southern extremity Horeb, with its granite rocks, runs almost precipitously to the height of 1200 or 1500 feet; and towards the west it is also shut in as with a wall by the equally precipitous spurs of Jebel Humr. The other plain, which is called <hi type="italic">Sebayeh</hi>, lies to the south-east of Sinai, or Jebel Musa in the more restricted sense; it is from 1400 to 1800 feet broad, 12,000 feet long, and is shut in towards the south and east by mountains, which rise very gently, and do not reach any considerable height. There are three wadys leading to this plain from er Rahah and the Sheikh valley. The most westerly of these, which separates Horeb-Sinai from Jebel Humr with Mount Catherine on the south, is called <hi type="italic">el Leja</hi>, and is a narrow defile full of great blocks of stone, and shut in towards the south like a <hi type="italic">cul de sac</hi> by Mount Catherine. The central one, which separates Horeb from Jebel Deir, is Wady <hi type="italic">Shoeib</hi> (Jethro valley), with the convent of Sinai in it, which is also called the Convent Valley in consequence. This is less confined, and not so much strewed with stones; towards the south it is not quite shut in, and yet not quite open, but bounded by a steep pass and a grassy mountain-saddle, viz., the easily accessible <hi type="italic">Jebel Sebayeh</hi>. The third and most easterly is the Wady es Sebayeh, which is from 400 to 600 feet broad, and leads form the Sheikh valley, in a southern and south-westerly direction, to the plain of the same name, which stretches like an amphitheatre to the southern slope of Sinai, or Jebel Musa, in the more restricted sense.
